You are not hungry, for your bellie's full; Lady, be rul'd by me: take the aduice A Doctor gaue a Gentleman of ate, That sent to him to know, whether Tobacco Were good for him or no: My friend quoth he, If thou didst neuer loue it, neuer take it; If thou didst euer loue it, neuer leaue it: So I to thee; if thou wert as thou hast Beene alwayes honest, I could wish thee still So to continue; but being a broken Lady, Your onely way's to make vse of your Talent, Farewell, I'le to my Countrey. Thou shouldst be mind: and durst I for my Head Euen in the open Court I'de challenge thee. But I haue so incenst th'offended Duke, And layd such heauy spots vpon her head, I cannot doo't wiht safety: methinkes this Child Doth looke me in the face, as if 'twould call Me Father, and but this suspected Stroza Stuft my too credulous eares with iealousies. For thee sweete Babe I'le sweare, that if not all, Part of my blood runnes in thy tender veynes, For those few drops I will not see the perish; Be it for her sake whom once I lou'd, And shall doe euer: Oh iniurious Stroza! I now begin to feare; for this sweete Babe Hath in his face no bastardy, but shewes A Princely semblance: but Stroza and the Duke, This will I keepe as charie as her honour, The which I prize aboue the Vniuerse. Though she were forc't to be unnaturall, I'le take to me this Infants pupillage; Nor yet resolu'd, till I a way haue found To make that perfect which is yet vnsound. My Father was a Noble Gentleman, Rank't with the best in Birth, and which did adde To all his other vertues, a bold Souldier; But when he dy'de— To tell you that, Were to exclaime vpon my Prince, my Countrey And their Ingratitude: For he being dead, With him our fortunes and our hopes both fail'd; My Mother loath to liue ignobly base, Where once she flourisht, hauing spent her meanes Not loosely nor in riot, but in the honour Of her dead Husband: left th'ingratefull Land, Rather to spend her yeares in pouerty, Mongst those that neuer knew her height of Fortune, Then with her thankelesse Friends and Countrey-men, Fled here to perish. We know you Lady, and your beauteous Daughter, Nay you shall spare your knee, You petition heere For Men and Money I making a free relation Of all your Husbands fortunes, how supplyes Haue beene delay'd, and what extremities He hath indurd at Naples dreadfull Seige; We know them all, and withall doe acknowledge All plentious blessings by the power of Heauen, By him wee doe obtaine, and by his valour Lady we greue he hath beene so neglected. Produce the witnesse; and behould, I stand The Champion for her honour, and will auerre Her Chaste, aboue degree; infinitely honest: Oh Prince! what, can you ground such iniury Vpon vaine heare-say? Speake for your selfe, take spirit Was the slaue neuer Christen'd, hath hee no name? Doe not stand off my Lord, If she be wrong'd, shee's not much behind-hand. What if you find her chaste? Then ioyne their hands. All goes not well, This iugling will be found, Then where am I then? would I were safe in Millaine. Here Matchiuell th'wast hatcht: Could not the same Planet inspire this pate of mine with some Rare stratagem, worthy a lasting Character: No, 'twill not be; my braine is at a non-plus, For I am dull. My Lord. I am turn'd Foole, Asse, Iddeott; Are they married? But the hell is, That they must lie together, ther's the Deuill. And then we are disgrac'd and sham'd. Why you would make A man—midwife, woo'd you? I haue no skill. Peace, interrupt me not, I ha'te: so to reuenge mee vpon her Whom most I hate. To Strumpet her 'twere braue. Youle make me mad my Lord: And in this sweet reuenge, I am not onely Pleas'd (with iust satisfaction for all wrongs) But the great Prince most palpably deceiu'd. If youle eate grapes vnripe, edge your owne teeth, Ile stay the mellow'd season, doo't your selfe, Vnlesse you giue me time for't. Peace, giue me way my Lord, so shall the Prince Bee palpably deceiu'd, Faire Iulia's honor Most prosperously deseru'd, The Duke my master, Freed from all blame, Wane hindred, Peace confirm'd, And I secur'd; Oh I am fortunate Beyond imagination! Hee was a a meere Asse That rais'd Troys Horse: 'twas a pritty structure. Synon, a foole, I can doe more With precious Gold, then hee with whining Teares. Pray my Lord, giue mee Fiue hundred crownes. See how you stand on trifles; when our liues, Your honour; all our fortunes lie a bleeding: What shall I haue the Gold? I know a desolate Lady, whom with Gold I can corrupt. But say I cannot win her, They bide the brunt of all, heere let them stay, With these fiue hundred Crownes Ile poast away. Lady bee happy, and from this blest houre Euer reioyce faire Virgin, for I bring you Gold, and Inlargement; with a recouerie Of all your former losse, and dignitie, But for a two houres labour: Nay, that no labour Nor toyle, but a meere pleasure. Haue wee not heere Too many • ares? You haue seene the Prince of Florence? Is he not for his Feature, Beauty, Goodnesse, The most Compleate? So absolute in all things. How happy doe you thinke that Lady then That shall Inioy him? Nay, that shall bee the first To prooue him, And exchange Virginitie, Were't not bright Lady a great happinesse? Loue him: What's she doth not, if shee haue eyes? Were I my selfe a Woman: I would lay My selfe a prostitute vnto the Prince: Shee is not wise that would refuse him Lady. To thee sweete Lady: I offer all these pleasures, Oh happie fate that hath selected mee To be your raiser: Lady take this gold, But that's not all: For there are greater honours Prepared for you; the Duke of Millaine doth Commend him to you: Iulia his daughter Hath in her honour late miscarried, Now 't lies in you to salue and make all good. Yes, in her, Shee hath the power to make the Duke her friend, Iulia her sister, and all Millaine bound To offer vp for her thier Orrisons. This night lie with the Prince In Iulia's stead: There's way made for you, Who would not woo, for what you are wooed too? You did Receiue them both, Haue you forgot sweet Lady, This very morning, that you gaue them both To me? The Princess ieasted, to see how You woo'd but take it. Where are they? they are— They are there— I poasted them To Millaine, sent them safe, dare you not trust my word By one oth' Princes Traine. I would I were in Turkey. From whom? whom, Parma? breake the bastards necke, As I would doe the Fathers, were hee here. I know of none. Right, I confest it; but your grace must know, 'Twas but to please your humour, which began To grow into some violence. That I did this? Hee lies below his entrayles, That dares to braue mee with such a proud affront: And in the honour of my Prince and Countrey I will approoue thee recreant. Saue mee, I will confesse; Is Parma heere? I falsely stuft thy head with Iealousies, And for some priuate ends of my reuenge, Disgrac'd the Generall, and set odds betwixt Lauretta and the Princesse: All these mischiefes Proceede from my suggestions. Is that your kindnesse? Giue me leane to liue, Bee't but to taynt his honour. No. Yes, and more too: I had the Gold from him, To bribe the Generalls daughter.
speeches.Iulia: It shall not, we are fixt and stand immou'd, And will be swaid by no hand. Submission is to me full recompence. He neuer exercis'd with me, I'm sure; I might haue layne as safe, free, and vntoucht, By any Lady liuing. I receiu'd none Sir. When? Where? 'Twas in my dreame then. Oh my perplexed heart! Pardon Sir, It well becomes my handling. Now haue I my desires: Had I withall, The Princely babe I boare.
Wherein O Heauen Haue I deseru'd your wrath, that you should thus Persue me? I haue searcht, indeed beyond My vnderstanding, but yet cannot finde? Wherein I haue offended by my chastity.
Must speake with the Duke, Ile doe neither, I come in haste with newes, Ha Milksop? know percullist gates Though kept with Pikes & Muskets, could nere kepe me out And dost thou thinke to shut me out with VVainscot? A Souldier, The Campe A mighty losse; a glorious victory Tis vncertaine Sir: But will you heare the best or bad newes first? Heare me then my Lord, We sack't the Citty after nine Moneths siege, Furnisht with store of all warres furniture, Our (neuer to be praisd enough) braue Generall Fought in the Cannons face, their number still Increast, but our diminisht; their souldiers pay Doubled, and ours kept backe: but we (braue spirits) The losse we had of Coyne, the more we tooke Vnto our selues of Courage, but when all Our furniture was spent euen to one day, And that to morrow we must be inforc't To raise a shameful siege, then stood our General (Our valiant Generall) vp, and breath'd vpon vs His owne vndaunted spirit, which spred through The Campe, return'd it doubly arm'd againe: For he did meane to lay vpon one shott His state and fortune, and then instantly He bad vs arme and follow: On then he went, We after him; oh! 'twas a glorious sight, Fit for a Theater of Gods to see, How we made vp and mauger all opposure, Made way through raging stormes of showring bullets; At last we came to hooke our ladders, and By them to skale. The first that mounted, was Our bold couragious Generall: after him Ten thousand, so we instantly were made Lords of the Citty, purchas'd in two houres After a nine Moneths siege: all by the valour Of our approued Generall. Oh that, which ten such Conquests Cannot make good, your worthy Generall. Sword? No alas, No sword durst byte vpon his noble flesh, Nor bullet raze his skinne: he whom War feared, The Cannon spar'd, no steele durst venture on. No Duke, 'twas thy vnkinde ingratitude Hath slaine braue Sforsa. I shall: This Citty seaz'd, his purpose was the spoyle To giue his Souldiers; but when his seal'd Commission He had vnript, and saw expresse command, To deale no farther then to victory, And that his great Authority was curb'd, And giuen to others, that respect their profit More then the worth of souldiers: euen for griefe, That he could neither furnish vs with pay Which was kept back, nor guerdon vs with spoile, What was about him he distributed, Euen to the best deseruers, as his garments, His Armes, and Tent, then some few words spake, And so opprest with griefe, his great heart brake. Pray on whom shall I attend? VVho is't must pay me? You sir? tell me, VVill it not cost me more the waiting for, Then the summe comes to when it is receiu'd? I doe but aske the question. You are a cunning slaue, And cowardly Courtier. Come will you pay me sir?
speeches.Duke: But which the greater? To Florence then wee'le streight dispatch Embassa dours, Stroza, bee't your care to mannage this high businesse. Oh to see How Parents loue descends: and how soe're The Children proue vngratefull and vnkinde, Though they deride, we weepe our poore eyes blinde. From Millaine.
Come fellow souldiers, doe you know the reason That we are summon'd thus vnto the house Of our dead Generall? He was a right And worthy Generall. Pay for three Moneths. I thanke your Ladiship.
Sure 'tis about Our pay. He was no lesse. VVhy Madam, For foure Moneths pay. I am treble satisfied.
But stand aside, here comes the Lady.
They are if please your Ladiship: though I was neuer Tawny-coate, I haue playd the summoners part, and the rest are already paide, onely these three attend your Ladiships re muneration. He was no lesse; and all you know hee was no more, well, had he liu'd, I had beene plac't in some house of office or other ere this time. Ey but Madam, I thinke he be no true souldier. Marry because he walkes without his Armes. I but Madam, this is a hard case being truly conside red, to giue away all, why your Shoe-maker, though he hath many other Tooles to worke with, he will not giue away his All. VVhy, say I had a peece of Meate, I had a mind to, I might perhaps giue away a Modicum, a Morcell, a Frag ment or so, but to giue away and bee a hungry my selfe, I durst not doo't for my Guts, or say I should meete with a friend that had but one Penny in his Purse, that should giue mee a Pot of Ale, that should drinke to me, and drinke vp all, I'le stand too't there's no Conscience in't. Shee might haue giuen away a little, and a little, but VVhen all is gone, what's left for me? Troth Madam, I could find in my heart to goe with you but for one thing. Marry we were both in the Tauerne together tother day— No Madam, but there stood at our elbow a pottle Pot— No Madam, but he stole the wine in the Pot, and drunke it off, And made himselfe so drunke hee be-pist himselfe: Your Ladyship could not be better be-pist in a Summers-day.
Madam, Hearts, Swords and hands, rest still At your command. May you be euer happy.
Because you are too liberall a Mistresse: and that's a fault seldome found among Ladies: For looke, you vse o giue away all, and I am all that is left; and I am affraide when you come into a strange Countrey, you'le giue away me too, so that I shall neuer liue to be my owne man. Why then I'le goe with you inspite of your teeth. That word all Stickes more in my stomacke then my victuals can: For in deede wee can get none to eate now; I told you, you were so prodiga'l we should pinch for't. Why this is the Duke-dome of Florence, and this is the Forrest where the hard-hearted Duke hunts many a Hart: and there's no Deere so deare to him, but hee'le kill it: as goodly a large place to starue in, as your Ladiship can de sire to see in a Summers day. How better starue then begge; all the Ladies of Florence shal neuer make me of that beleefe. I had rather beg a thousand times, then starue once, doe you scorne begging? Your betters doe not, no Madam; get me a Snap-sacke, I'le to Florence: I'le make all the high wayes ring of me with for the Lords sake. I haue studied a Prayer for him that giues, and a Poxe take him that giues nothing: I haue one for the Horse-way, another for the Foote-way, and a third for the turning-ftile. No Madam, begging is growne a gentleman like Calling here in our Countrey. You had better keepe your Gold, and trust to my begging Oratory, yet this is the worst they can say to mee, that I am my Ladies Bottle-man. Nay, now I thinke I haue fitted you with a Cup of N • psi •• t • . What am I? Nay what art thou? I thinke you le proue little better then a smell-smocke, That can finde out a pretty wench in such a Corner. What if he be? he may loue a Wench as well as a nother man. A bottle of Wine and a Manchet that my Lady sent me for. Yes, when? can you tell? doe you thinke I am such an Asse, to part so lightly with my liquor? Know thou my friend, before I could get this bottle fill'd, I was glad to change a piece of Gold, and call for the rest againe. And doe you thinke I'le loose my liquor, and haue no Gold nor rest a gaine? Not so my Friend, not so. Madam, will you giue me a Licence to sell VVine? I could get no P • ate in the Forrest but a woodden Dish. The bottome of the bottle is at your seruice Sir, Shall you and I part stakes? I had rather you had broke my pate then my draught, but harke you Sir, are you as a man should say, a belonger to? Oh ignorant! are you a follower? A Seruing-man I take it. I desire you the more complement: I haue the cour tesie of the Forrest for you. That's to bring me to the Buttery hatch, and neuer make me drinke. How now sawce-boxe, know your manners: was not I Gentleman vsher before you came? Am not I hee that did the bottle bring? Come Ladies follow me. Nay, nay, the case is alter'd with mee since you saw me last: I was neuer in any hope to purchase any other suite then that I wore yesterday; but now I can say Ecce sig num, the case is alter'd. Now euery begger comes vpon me with good Gentleman, good Gentleman: when yesterday Gen tlemen would haue shun'd the way for feare I should haue begg'd of them. Then comes another vpon mee with good your Worship, good your Worship, then doe I double my fyles, and cast him a 〈◊〉 two pence. Tnou say'st true; for he hath chang'd our woodden Dishes to Si uer Coblets: goodly large Arras that neuer yet deseru'd hanging, he hath caus'd to be hang'd round about the Chamber: My Lady and Mistresse, now my Lady and Mistresse lyes ouer head and cares in Downe and Feathers: well, if they be rui'd by me, I would haue them to keepe their beds. Oh dull ignorant ! I meane knowing how hard they haue bin lodg'd in the Forrest; I would not haue them sell a way their beds, and lie vpon the boords. Right: for yeasterday thou wouldst haue taken me for a very Clowne, a very Clowne; and now to see, to see.— Madam. Shee talkes: Now, if shee should be enuamored of my comely shape; for I haue (as they say) such a foolish yong and relenting heart I should neuer say her nay, I should ne uer weare off this stand further off. No, I'le assure your Ladiship 'tis beaten Sattin. Your Ladiship hath coniur'd me, and I will auoide Satan. So hoe Mistris Madam, yonder is the Prince, and two or three Gentlemen come riding vpon the goodliest Hor ses that euer I set my eyes vpon: and the Princes Horse did no sooner see me, but he weeighed and wagg'd his tayle: now I thinking he had done it to take acquaintance of me, said a gaine to him, Gramery Horse; so I left them, and came to tell your Ladiship. Oh my Lord, my Lord, Are you close at it? and you too crabbed Age, and you the—there's Rods in pisse for some of you. Oh my Lord, there's a Nobleman come from the Court to speake with you. And you can but keepe your leggs close, Let him rend any thing else and spare not. I confesse it; but whether you haue seru'd him well, or no, there hangs a Tale. Some three miles off, here in the Forrest, not halfe an houres riding. You shall not want directions to find the place, come when you will, you shall be most heartily—poyson'd. And behang'd, Monsieur Stroza, whose description My Muse hath included in these few lines; Stroza, Thy Head is of a compely Block, And would shew well, crown'd with the combe of Cock: His Face an Inne, his Brow a sluttish Roome, His Nose the Chamberlaine, his Beard the Broome, Or like New-market Heath, that makes theeues rich, In which his Mouth stands iust like Deuills-ditch And so farewell to your worship, graue Mounsieur Stroza, For I must about my market. Maddam, yonder's a Gentleman comes to speake with you in all hast. Marry, I would intreat your Lady-ship to turne away My fellow Ierom, for I thinke hee's No true man. Yes and their man too; all that's left of him. Your Lordship hath bin vp already, when shee was downe: I hope if the thing you wott of goe no worse forward then it hath hegun, and that you take charge of my young Lady, you neede not bee altogether vnmindfull of her Gentleman-Vsher.
My blushes must speake for me. And yet but what's your owne Sir, I am serious, And it will ill become your Oathes and Vowes To iest at my vndoeing. In doing thus, you should vndoe me quite. You haue dishonoured me, and by your flattery Haue rob'd me of my chaste Virginity: Yet ere I yeelded, we were man and wife, Sauing the Churches outward Ceremony. Can this be found in man? Oh miserable, Let me but reckon vp ten thousand ills My loosenesse hath committed, the aspersion And scandalous reputation of my Childe, My Father too, 'tmust come vnto his care, Oh— Away. That all those blacke occurrents should conspire, And end in my disgrace. If all men were such, I should be sorry that a man begot me, Although he were my father. How my Father! then doe one thing For me your Daughter Instantly then draw your sword And pierce me to the heart. Nor I my selfe so well, as to desire A longer life: if you be then my Father, Punish a sinne that hath disgrac't your Daughter, Scandald your blood, and poyson'd it with mud. See, I am strumpeted, A bastard issue growes within my wombe. Prince Parmaes.
Oh misery beyond comparison! When saue the Heauens we haue no roofe at all To shelter vs.
speeches.Wife: What place may wee call this? what Clime? what Prouince? Yet here, since no man knowes vs, no man can Deride our misery: better dye staru'd, Then basely begge. I haue yet one poore piece of Gold reseru'd, Step to the Vi • lage by and fetch some Wine. Here's a strange change: we must be patient, Yet can I not but weepe thinking on thee. It seemes the Duke is Hunting in the Forrest, Here let vs rest our selues, and listen to Their Tones, for nothing but mishap here lies; Sing thou faire Childe, I'le keepe tune with my eyes. Wee're discouered, Daughter arise. Pardon Great Sir, this our neglect of duty Vnto a Prince so gracious and compleate In vertuous indowments. P • ace sirrah, 'tis the Prince. Fill to the Prince Lauretia. Sir. Sirrah. He's a mirrour, and deserues a name Amongst the famous Worthies. Why sigh you? Loue Daughter? I aduise you curbe your sence in time, Or you will bring your selfe into the way Of much dishonour. For this I loue thee. Royall Sir, 'Tis beyond hope or merit. Try the fooles counsell daughter, but bee sure To forfit, and to pay. Child I must chide you, you giue too much way vnto this humour: It alters much your beautie. Away, your foolerie's vnseasonable, Weele not beleeue you. Helpe to support her. No true man, Why? And hee stole some Plate? And hee stole the Pot? Shee tooke so little rest last night, my Lord I thinke shee is scarce well.
speeches.Prince: This way the voyce was, let vs leaue the Chace. Here's beauty mixt with teares, that pouerty Was neuer bred in Cottage: I'le farther question Their state and fortune. What are you gentle Creatures? Nay answere not in teares. If you by casuall losse, or by the hand Of Fortune haue beene crusht beneath these sorrowes, He demands your griefe That hath as much will as ability To succour you, and for your owne faire sake; Nay beautious Damsell, you neede not question that. Arise sweete, pray your name? Faire Laure • t • , you shall be henceforth ours, Oh Mounsieur! I ne're saw where I could loue Till now. Well Mounsieur, well; when e're I match, pray Heauen, We loue so well: but loue and toyle hath made vs Euen somewhat thirsty, would we had some Wine. What hast thou there? Thou ne're couldst come to vs in better time, Reach it vs Mounsieur. Yes sweete with thee in any thing: you know Wee are a Prince, and you shall be our taster. Sirrah, conduct those Ladies to the Lodge, And tell the Keeper we haue stor'd for him, A better fortune; you shall heare further from vs, You vsher them. Oh gentle Friend, Why was I borne high? but to raise their hopes That are deiected: so much for my bounty. It is with no intent To make the Maide my wife, because I know Her fortunes cannot equall mine. Still thou mistak'st, mine Is honourable loue, and built on vertue; Nor would I for the Emperours Diademe, Corrupt her whom I loue. Come Mounsieur, night steales on, not many yeares Shall passe me, but I purpose to reuisite This my new Mistresse, my auspicious fate To thee my happy loue I consecrate. Now my faire Friend. Looke Mounsieur, Can she be lesse then Noble? nay deserues she Thus habited, to be tearm'd lesse then Royall, What thinkst thou Mounsieur? Right courteous Lady, Our bounty is too sparing for your worth, Yet such as 'tis accept it. I prithee Mounsieur, A little comp ement with that old Lady, Whilst I conferre with her. And haue you ne're a loue then? Pray acquaint me with him, And for thy sake I'le giue him state and Honours, And make him great in Florence. Is he of birth? How now my Lauretta? I prithee sweete where liues he? Honour me so much As let me know him. Must? then I will. Is he of presence sweete? Honour me so much then, as let me know him. Thee, loue I will In all things: wherefore study you? Harme? there's none can come from thee Lauretta, Thou art all goodnesse, nay confesse it sweete. Mounsieur what are those? Whence are these Lords? Their businesse Royall Sir? Vnto my bed my Lord? I am not so affraide of spirits Sir, But I can lye alone without a bed-fellow. Marry my Lord? But is she faire? I figh Lauretta, cause I cannot chuse. Ile tell thee Loue, strange newes: I must be married. Why doe you weepe? You blam'd mee now for sigh ing: Why doe you melt in teares? Sweet what's the cause? And as I told thee Sweete; I must bee married, My Father and the State will haue it so; And I came instantly to tell the newes To thee Lauretta; As to one, from whom I nothing can conceale. Must you? But when's the day? The tenth of the next moneth. But doe you loue him? How happie are you aboue mee faire friend, That must inioy where you affect? When I Am tide to others fancies: It was your promise That I should know him further. 'Tis Iulia, The Duke of Millaines daughter: Why change your Face? Looke to her safety, not for the Crowne Of Florence I would haue her perish. Oh Friend, that I should change my Royaltie To weaknesse now: I doe thinke this lodge A Pallace, and this Beautious Mayden-head Of greater worth then Iulia. Thy newes. Whence? The Millaine Princesse is betroathed; deflowred, Not worthy of your loue, beleeue this true Vpon a Prince his word; when you, shall bed her, And find her flawd in her Virginitie, You shall haue cause to thinke vpon his loue From whom you had this caution; But doe it with that Princely management, Her honour bee not slandered: Hee that loues, Admires, and honours you: Where's hee that brought this Letter? Poast after; bring him backe, Could hee not set his hand to 't— How now, the newes? Thou hast lost mee quite. Mounsieur reade there, What will confound thee: Oh if shee bee vnchast! Could they find none but mee to worke vpon. If shee bee Chast, How shall I wrong her, to question her faire Vertues? But if shee bee not right? I wrong my Honor, Which after marriage, how shall I recall? Yes: Oh how am I perplext! Come, Ile to Court, Ile not bee sway'd: Were shee a Potent Queene, Where Counsell fayles mee, Ile once trust to spleene. Pardon Lords, I haue stay'd you long, your blessing royall Father. My custome is, euer to rise before A womans houre: Now heare me speake my Lords, I'm married to a Lady, whose chaste honour, Reports and false Suggestions, did inforce me To call in publike question; but that we leaue Vnto our last nights rest. Last night. In your Bed. Being broad awake. 'Twas well put off: 'Tis strange shee's so forgetfull: I prethee Stroza Where are they? Where? Why studdy you? Where man? See which o' the Traine is wanting. Giue this Gentleman A 100. crownes: This will much grace our banquet. Wee are hee. Excuse mee Sir, I know him not: But if I much mistake not, Wee are late indebted to you for a present. 'Tis false, I neuer imbrac'd saue with one, And her, I found to bee most truely chast. Yes. Wee are pleased. Tell mee Stroza, Was Iulia chaste? Did her Father know it? At hand my Lord: Mounsieur conduct them hither? This the Maide, To whom I am so bound? But by your fauour Sir, This must bee our owne charge. You crowne me with your wishes, Royall father; My Mistris first, and next my bed-fellow, And now my Bride most welcome. Excellent Sir, Imbrace the Millaine Duke, whil'st I change hand With Princely Parma; Iulia, once my Wife? Backe to your husband I returne you chast: Mounsieur, bee still our friend: You our kind Mother: And let succeeding Ages, thus much say: Never was Maiden-head better giuen away.
Behold my Lord two sad deiected Creatures Throwne on the humble verdure. How now my Lord, remember pray, What you are to this poore deiected Maide. How now sirrah, what are you? Your bottle quickly sirrah, come I say. There's Gold sir. Lady, thankes: I feare me he is caught, But if he be, my Counsell must diuert him. T • cie's more Gold for you. Your purpose Sir, is to loue this Lady, And hazard all your hopes. But for your loue. Then 'twere more dishonorable To strumpet her. Braue Prince I'me glad That ere I kept thy Company. Faith my Lord, I neuer loue a woman for her habite, When sir I loue, I'le fee my lone starke naked. I thanke you Sir: See, you would make me a sir Panderus, Yet farre as I can see you, I will trust you. Sweete Lady, how long is't—nay keepe that hand, Since those fierce warres 'twixt Florence and great Millaine Nay that hand still. Good Sir make haste, lest I be challeng'd for you. Embassadours my Lord. How's this my Lord? They offer loue and beauty, which being both So freely offer'd, doe deserue acceptance, Come my Lord, Lay by these idle thoughts, and make you ready To entertaine your Bride. Fled my Lord. Hee's fled vpon a milke white Gennet Sir, Seeming t'out strip the winde, and I—lost him. What meanes this passions Sir? It confounds mee my Lord. Right. 'Tis certaine. My Lord, yeeld to your father, lest you draw His wrath vpon you. What doe you not like your bed-fellow, my Lord; That you are vp so soone? Millaine should know, were it my case my Lord, A better Prince then hee should not wrong me. Excellent Villaine! I shall my Lord. None my Lord. Why, t'was confest. I can forbeare no longer; Impudent Stroza, Thou art a Villaine, periur'd, and forsworne: That Duke dishonourable; and shee vnchast: Besides, thou hyredst a Virgin in her roome; (Slaue as thou art) to bosome with the Prince; Gau'st her fiue hundred Crownes. That this is true, I will maintaine by combat. Yeeld thy selfe recreant villaine, or thou dy'st. I shall Sir.
Sweete if the Prologue To thy sad passion mooue thus: what will the Sceane And tragicke act it selfe doe? Is thatt Gentlewoman Your Mother sweete? Pray of what Prouince? What fortune there? Nay, proceede beauteous Lady, How was your Father stil'd? More then her Charming beauty Her passion moues me: where inhabit you? Beneath these Trees? Gentle Creature, Had you not told me that your Birth was Noble, I should haue found it in your face and gesture. Mounsieur. Goe winde thy Horne abroad, and call to vs Some of our traine: we pitty these two Ladies, And we will raise thier hope: Cheere you old Madam, You shall receiue some bounty from a Prince. Who keepes the Lodge below? Command him to remoue, and instantly We giue it to these Ladies: besides, adde Vnto our Guest three thousand pounds a yeare: We'le see it furnisht too with Plate and Hangings. 'Las pretyt Maide, your father's dead you say, We'le take you now to our owne Patronage, And trust me Lady, whiel wee're Prince of Florence, You shall not want nor foode, nor harborage. Why my Lauretta? By all my hopes I haue in Florence, would thou wert a Dutchesse, That I might court thee vpon equall tearmes; Or that I were of low deiected fortunes, To ranke with thee in Birth: for to enioy Thy beauty, were a greater Dowre then Florence Great Duke-dome. Now sir, the newes? Mounsieur, vpon my life 'tis some Embassadour. No worthy Friend, for me thou shalt not suffer, At our best leasur'd houres we meane to visite you; Now giue me leaue to take a short fare-well. What, and as Charte? Would you had, For both were rauisht. That I am yours: The States; and if you please So to dispose me, hers: what ere she be, Come friend, I must impart my Loue this newes, Or it will rend my heart. Stay till we be resolu'd. Sir, so we haue heard. O Heauen, how am I perplext! Well, since I must, I will: Your pardon, Royall Father: Yours faire Princesse: And yours great Duke: If I shall find my self truely to haue err'd, I shall confesse your chastity much iniur'd. Oh good morrow Lady, I come to tell you newes! Not till I see my deeds. Your Masters name? Parma speake, and if thy speech was bent to mee? Parma proceede. Will Parma fight? I heere protest, wee parted both, as cleere, As at our first encounter. Willingly. Then Prince Parma, With your words Ile proceed. 'Tis fit all Iustice hee not quite exil'd, That hee that wedds the Mother keepe the child. Sweete arise.
A belonger to? what's that sir? I seldome goe before when my betters are in place. Right sir. And I haue the courtesie of the Court for you sir. Come Ladies will you walke? Sirrah, thou may st thanke the Prince for this. Why wouldst thou haue them lye a bed all day? Oh now I vnderstand you sir. 'Tis true: 'tis strange to see how Apparrell makes or maries.
speeches.Milleine: Forbeare my Lords for a few priuate words: Faire Daughter, wee'le not chide you farther now Nor adde vnto your blushes: by our rude Reproofes your faults are couered with these your sighes, Since all your fire of lust is quencht in ashes.
I'le not haue it question'd. I striue to salue thy honour, and thou seek'st To publish thy disgrace: my study is Where I may picke thee out a noble Husband, To shadow these dishonours, and keepe thee From the like scandall. Oh name him not thou strumpet. There's a Prince of noble hopes and fortunes, The Prince of Florence: what if I sent to him About a speedy Marriage? for I feare, Delay may breed strange doubts. Stroza. Laid out? What, and suspectlesse? My excellent friend, For this wee'le bosome thee: your counsel Stroza, Our Daughter's growne to yeares, and we intend To picke her out a Husband, in whose issue Her name may flourish, and her honours liue: But where my Lords May we prouide a match to equall her?
speeches.1 Lord: Ferrara hath a faire and hopefull Heire. In fame no whit inferiour.
speeches.2 Lord: And so hath Mantua. But in state Many degrees excelling: aime no further Sir, if that may be accepted.
speeches.3 Lord: How do you prize the Noble Florentine?
speeches.Clow,: Ey, ey; thou may'st get much vnderstanding by keeping my company: But Sir, does not the new Gowne the Prince sent my Mistresse, become her most incompa rably?
Speake the true Tenor of your Embassie. 'Tis granted: onely our Sonnes consent Is wanting: but see here, he wisht for comes. About a match, Which if you't please, we highly shall applaud. They offer you a faire and vertuous Princesse Vnto your bed: 'Tis the faire Princesse Iulia you must Marry. I marry must you Sir, Or you diuorce your selfe from our deare loue. Ther's in that dish, some Morrall. There should be more in't, then a feasting dish; What's here, a Child?
speeches.Florence: We doe conceite you: But for the Dowre you craue? Princes, forbeare: First see the Issue of the former Combat, Before more blood you hazard. Iniuries, Beyond the thought of man. But Peeres, the Virgin that this Stroza hired To Iustifie thee wrongs? Of what birth is that Lady? With which we are pleas'd.
Faithfully As we intend it: But you first shall taste The bounty of our Court, with royall Presents Both to the Duke your master, and the Princesse; It done, prepare we for this great solemnity, Of Hymeneall Iubilies. Fixt is the day, Wherein rich Florens shall her pompe display. What meanes our sonne?
Onely to you, of all the Millaine Peeres, I dare expose my safety. I doe not doubt it: But I pray you tell me, since I left the Court, How is my absence taken? But of the Princesse Iulia? Brauely manag'd, The Duke I see was more kind to her fame, Then to his prettie grand-childe; well Ile salt it all, But what thinke you if after all I should Send Letters to her, or Ambassadors? I should not win her, for I know Th'aue her heart in bondage. No more: Pray leaue mee Sir. To bee married, Ruimus in vestitum semper, I did neglect her, but being deni'd, I doate vpon her beautie: Methinkes 'tis fit, If I begot the Child? I wed the Mother: The Prince, I pitie hee should bee so wrong'd, And I the Instrument: Now helpe mee braine, That neare was wont to fayle mee: 'Tis decreed Something to Plot, although I faile to speede. The Prince, the Prince, I come to seeke the Prince, and was directed Vnto this place. A Letter. Reade, the Contents will shew you; their eyes are from mee, and I must hence. And Parma? It was a gift, I should bee loath to part with, But vpon good conditions. Am I then To all a stranger: Doe you not know mee Lady? Ere I proceede, let mee behold this babe; Nere a Nurse heere? Pray hand it you sweete Lady, Till I find out a Mother. Then Florence know, thou hast wrong'd me beyond, thought; Shipwrackt my Honour, and my Fame; nay strumpeted Her, whom I tearme my Bride. Then It maintaine: Hast thou a Wife heere? Then Ile approoue her to bee none of thine, That thou hast fetch't her from anothers armes. Nay more, that shee's vnchast? And wee content. Yes, heere wee are. Resolue mee first? Was Iulia found Chast? Then I accept her, If you my Lord Bee pleas'd so to part with her. See Iulia, Whom thy hard-hearted Father doom'd to death, My care hath still Conserued, Imbrace it Lady; Nay, 'tis thy owne nere feare it.
In these armes My Lord, you are Sanctuared. Of the Duke, With much distaste. I will: Pray Sir Regard your safety.
speeches.Lord: Full two Moneths Shee kept her Chamber, grieuously distracted, They say, meere griefe for your departure hence. Why worthy Prince, Haue you not heard the newes: Shee hath beene offered Vnto the Florentine, the match accepted, And the Nuptiall day the tenth of the next Moneth.
speeches.Clowne: I wonder you should bee so sad and melanchollie, Ile lay a yeeres wages before hand Ile tell your disease, As well as any Doctor in Florence, and Let me but feele your pulse. That's no matter whether I bee a foole or a phisitian, If I loose, Ile pay, that's certaina. Nay, I must feele your pulse first, for if a Womans pulse bee neere a place, I know there's few heere of my yeeres but would bee glad to turne Doctors. Nay, if it bee nothing else, Ile fetch that will cure you presently. Oh young Mistris, where are you, the Prince, The Prince. Where is hee? Why at the Court; where should hee bee? I did but doo't to make you smile: Nay, Ile tickle you for a Doctor: Madam I haue a yeeres wages before hand. No marrie is hee not. Nay Madam, the Prince is come. If you will not beleeue mee, will you beleeue these?
Away, you are a foole, and trouble vs. Now sir, your skill. Now sir, you see I doe not smile. Oh Mother, doe you heare the newes, the Prince, The Prince is comming. Where is hee, oh where? Is hee not come then? Welcome my Lord: And wherefore doe you sigh? Nor could I chuse, should you but sigh againe. Married my Lord! Nay, nothing. Why should you grieue For that? For I, my Lord, must haue a Husband too. When's yours my Lord? The selfe same day, And selfesame houre that you inioy your loue, My Princely Husband I must then inioy. Not my selfe more deere. You shall see him That day, as richly habited as the great Heire of Florence: But royall Sir, what's shee That you must bed then? That shee that hates mee most should liue to inioy Him I affect best: O my ominous fate, I thought to haue hid mee from thee in these desarts, But thou dost dogg mee euery where. Admit him in. Wee would bee priuate sirra, And therefore leaue vs. Yes, I haue. All this is granted. I wish that nappinesse were mine alone, Oh my faint heart: Passion ouer-swayes me quite, But hide thy griefe Lauretta: Sir, you 'le make Me fall in loue with him: Were I his equall, I then should iudge him worthy of no lesse. Good Sir bee briefe: To what pray tends these speeches? Good Sir bee plaine. Doe you not blush, when you deliuer this Praye tell the Duke, all Women are not Iulia, And though wee bee deiected, thus much tell him, Wee hold our honour at too high a price, For Gold to buy. Sir bee answered, If Iulia bee disloyall: Let her bee found So by the Prince she wedds: Let her be branded With the vile name of strumpet: Shee disgrac'd Mee, that nere thought her harmes; publikely strucke mee, Nay in the Court: And after that, procur'd My banishment: These Iniuries I reap't By her alone, then let it light on her. My blood rebells against my reason, and I no way can withstand it: 'Tis not the Gold Mooues mee, but that deere loue I beare the Prince, Makes me neglect the credit and the honour Of my deare Fathers house: Sir, what the Duke desires I am resolued to doe his vtmost will. Good Mother speake not, for my word is past. And cannot bee recall'd, Sir will you away? I am resolute. The Prince is fast, all done. And for my part, it was not much amisse, Because my Lord the Prince had such content Which caus'd him giue his Charter to my hand, The full assurance of faire Iulia's dowre: Day gins to breake, and I must to the Lodge. Oh what a griefe it was to leaue the Prince! But leaue those thoughts: These Gifts to me assign'd, Are nothing worth the Iem I left behind. They are wellcome to me my Lord. So we haue heard it rumor'd Trew My Lord, I did. And lay with him last night. That you may soone coniecture by this gift. Some few my Lord, amongst the rest, this diamond Hee put vpon my finger. Sir, ten thousand crownes by th' yeere. See here, My Lord, Sir, Is not that sufficient for a dowry? Pardon great Prince; for all that loue you spake To Iulia, you whisper'd in my eare: Shee is vnchast; which, lest you should haue found, Her father sent mee here, fiue hundred crownes By Stroza; but neither his gold, nor all His sly temptations, could one whit mooue mee; Onely the loue I euer bare your honour, Made me not prise my owne. No lust full appetite Made me attempt such an ambitious practise, As to aspire vnto your bed my Lord. Great Sir, I shall. Royall Princesse, I still shall be your hand-maide.
My soule did leape within, to heare the Prince But nam'd: It started euery ioynt.
Let me see, the Prince is to bee married to morrow, and my young Mistris meanes to keepe a Feast in the Forrest, in honour of his wedding at the Court: Now am I sent as Ca terer into the City to prouide them victualls, which they charg'd me to buy; no ordinary fare, no more it shall, and therefore I haue cast it thus; First and foremost, wee will haue—(yes downe it shall) we will haue a Gammon of Bacon roasted, and stufft with Oysters; And sixe Black-Puddings to bee serued vp in Sorrell-sops; A pickell'd shoulder of Mutton, and a surloyne of Beefe in White-broth, so much for the first course. Now, for the second, we will haue a Cherry-Tart cut into Rashers and broyled; A Custard Carbonado'd on the coales; A liue Eele swimming in clowted Creame; And sixe Sheepes-heads baked, with the hornes peer •• gout of the pasty-crust. The morrall is, because it is a wedding dinner. What, my old Polititian? hee that vndermin'd my old Lady and my yong Mistris? now that I could find but one stratagem to blow him vp; I would tosse him, I would blanket him i'th Ayre, and make him cut an Italian caper in the Clouds: These Polititians can doe more execution with a pen, in their studies, then a good Souldier with his sword in the field, but he hath spi'd mee. And you too, I should haue knowne, but whether for a friend, or no, ther's the question?
Not to be gull'd by the best Prince in Europe; Much lesse by Millaine.
Sir, be plaine with vs. Hers. I came in termes of Honour, Brought with me, all my comforts here on earth, My daughter; to bestow her on thy son: Poore Lady, innocently comming, forsaking all, Father and Countrey, to betake her selfe Vnto his bosome; and is she for all this, Branded with shame?
I much suspect that Ladies Chastity. I haue said. Now heare my protestations: I receiue This Ladies hand on these Conditions; If you, my Lord, her father, or her selfe, Know her selfe faulty, Oh confesse it here, Before the Ceremonies fasten on me: for if hereafter I find you once corrupted? by this right hand, My future hopes, my Fathers royalty, And all the honours due vnto our house, He haue as many liues and heads for it, As he hath Manners Castles, Liues and Towres; It shall be worthy to be bookt in Chronicles Of all strange tongues: And therefore beautious Lady, As you esteeme a Prince his name or honour, That youd be a Mecenas vnto vertue; If in the least of these you guilty be, Pull backe your hand. If chaste? she shall be dearer farre to me. Then my owne soule: I will respect her honour, Equall with that of my great Ancestours; All this I vow, as I am Prince and vertuous. Shee's mine: Set forwards then. Oh friend, was neuer man blest with a Bride So chast! I'me fearce my selfe, till this be knowne To my faire Forrest friend: Lett's mount away, The nights quite spent; and now begins the day. Good morrow Lady: Wher's your daughter pray? Pray may wee see her? You know the Princesse Iulia was suppos'd to bee Adulterate— Oh but faire friend, she was indeed bely'd! And I this morning rose from her chast bed: But wherefore sweete cast you that blushing smile? But you haue broak promise with me: For you told me That the same day and houre I took my Bride, You should Inioy a Princely Husband. And are you married then? Is hee oft fortunes? What haue you then, some tokens that were his? You amaze mee! Yet Rings may bee alike: If then your husband Bee of such state and fortunes, What dowre are you allotted. I gaue no more vnto my Iulia. But where is the security you haue For the performance of it? This is the Indenture that I gaue to Iulia; Preethee Lauretta, but resolue me true, How came you by this Charter? Rise, dee not weepe, Oh I am strangely rapt Into deepe strange confusion? I haue bethought already how to be are mee; This Charter and this Ring, faire Loue, keepe you; And when I send for you, you shall repaire Vnto the Court: This all I shall inioyne you. Come Mounsieur, now 'tis cast, Reuenge neere rules, so it be found at last. I doe protest, my Lords, I bosom'd with As true and chaste a Virgin, as ere lodg'd Within a Princes armes; All this I vow As I am Royall. Sweet, will you tel mee that? With which you did receiue a Ring the Duke My father gaue me. Nay, looke not you deiected beautious Bride, For this is done onely to honour you. Sure spare't for the Mothers sake; t'was sent to vs: Which of the trayne is wanting? Stroza, where is this Charter and the Ring? A strife, that nought saue combat can deside, The cause so full of doubts, and intricate. See, they are both arm'd, and euenly, without odds, Saue what the iustice of the cause can yeeld. Know Parma, thou hast kindled such a Flame, That all the Oceans billowes scarce can quench: Bee that onr quarrells ground.
Sonne, Sonne, you wrong Your selfe and me too, to accuse a Lady Of such high birth and fame; vnlesse you confesse Your selfe to haue err'd, you needs must forfeit vs. Sir, hee neuer sleepes Longer then th'day, nor keepes his bed by Sunne: 'Tis not the lone of the fairest Lady liues, Can make him leaue his morning exercise.
My daughters honour? Oh let me alone Stroza. My hearts no closet for reuenge; tis done. Stroza. Oh now, or neuer Stroza! Yes, and the Prince after the Ceremonie, Imbrac'd her louingly. And then— Canst thou not help't man? Stroza, awake, th'art drowsie. Counsell aduise me. The time runs on, Thinke on my honor Stroza. But thinke with mine, on thine owne safety Stroza. O deare Stroza, Helpe now, or neuer! Oh mee! Oh my tormented soule! What to doe with them man? Thy purpose preethee? There are fiue hundred Crownes, Snroza bethinke thee what thou vndertak'st, Such an Act, would make huge Atlas bend his head Vnto his heele. Thou art our trusty Counsellor; if this passe 〈◊〉 We're past all feare: What is she preethee? What? But gaue you charge Assoone as ere the Prince was fast asleepe, That shee should rise and giue place to our daughter? How long she stayes, I faine would be a bed; Pray heauen shee doe not fail By him asleepe, and so forget her selfe. What, not yet? had she with Parma beene a bed so long, It would haue more perplext mee. Step in her place; Nay when? and counterfeit sleepe presently. Who saw the Prince last? Is't a custome with him To rise thus early? Stroza, I feare too. Would I were on horse-backe. Comming from him, Meethinks it should be season'd with some strange And dangerous poyson: Touch't not, my Lord. Heare him not speake, I charge thee by thine honor? Touch it not, I charge thee on my blessing. Damne him for it. Which wee 'le no longer striue with, since the hea uens haue laid that ope most plaine and palpable, which most wee thought to conceale. The Generalls Wife and Daughter. Euen the least Enuy can speake, Shee is a Souldiers Daughter, Decended from a noble parentage. You haue both: Sure, sure, the heauens for our Ingratitude, To noble Sforza, onr braue generall, Hath sau'd crost our proceedings: which to recompence, Wee'le take you vnto our best patronage.

speeches.Lau: Your words like musick, please me with delight, Beyond imagination: Offered to vs? Being exil'd our Countrey, and our friends, Therefore good sir, delay not with long complement, But tell these hopes more plaine.
